item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Iran and Ukraine are strategically sinking their rivals at sea
item.description:
How Iran and Ukraine are strategically sinking their rivals at sea

Submitted by Omar Ashour on Mon, 07/06/2026 - 20:54
Through a combination of tactics, both countries have managed to keep superior fleets at bay, dealing significant blows to the US and Russia
Images released by Ukrainian authorities in November 2025 show what they say are sea drone attacks on oil tankers in the Black Sea (Security Service of Ukraine/AFP)
Off

The Iran war may be fought primarily remotely via the air, but its strategic outcome is increasingly being decided at sea. 

The latest strikes and counterstrikes have clarified rather than altered that central fact. Washington may escalate through a ground intervention, wider attacks on Iran’s critical infrastructure, or a strike against the deeply buried nuclear-linked complex at Pickaxe Mountain in Isfahan province.

Each option could inflict further damage and expand the war. None, however, is likely to eliminate Iran’s distributed maritime architecture or make the Strait of Hormuz strategically irrelevant.

Last month, the Iran war’s political afterlife was being staged in Tehran. The funeral ceremonies for the country’s former supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, were not merely rituals of mourning; they became a demonstration of institutional continuity after shock, decapitation and bombardment. 

That resilience was not produced by the sea alone, but the maritime domain helped to preserve it. 

Iran could absorb severe punishment from its skies because it retained coercive leverage at sea: mined routes, controlled passage, slowed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, warnings to vessels using “unauthorised” corridors, and the continuing threat that any air campaign against Iran would generate a maritime bill for Washington, Gulf capitals, insurers and global energy markets. 

The administrations of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu failed to force Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s new supreme leader, to drink from the late Ruhollah Khomeini’s famous “chalice of poison”. 

In a way, Trump drank from a smaller chalice of his own, after falsely claiming to have “destroyed 100 percent of Iran’s military capability”. The 14-point interim deal with Iran looked less like surrender than the diplomatic translation of a maritime fact: Iran only had to make Hormuz costly enough to move from a war to a table. And now from the table to the war again.

The result was not victory in the classical sense. It was strategic sabotage of Washington’s war aims, converted into bargaining power.

The campaign exposed the gap between operational dominance and strategic victory. American and Israeli airpower could punish Iran’s air forces, damage fixed infrastructure, and kill senior figures. But regime collapse, missile disarmament, and military incapacitation did not follow. 

The ground forces of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, known as the Artesh, remained solid. More importantly, the part of Iran’s force design least dependent on pristine airspace - its littoral naval and missile-drone complex - retained both coercive value and combat effectiveness.

Lessons of the past

Military history should have warned against overconfidence. In Hanoi in April 1975, Colonel Harry G Summers Jr told his North Vietnamese counterpart: “You know, you never defeated us on the battlefield.” Colonel Tu’s reply was: “That may be so, but it’s also irrelevant.” 

That exchange should haunt any assessment of the 2026 Iran war. Its logic is simple: tactical dominance, even with air superiority, does not decide a war if it fails to break the adversary’s strategic leverage and steely will.

The same logic applies at sea. During the 1980s tanker war, Iran was already exhausted by seven years of war with Iraq when the US entered the fray more directly through a series of operations: Earnest Will, Prime Chance, Nimble Archer, and finally, Praying Mantis. 

The last of these was a clear US operational victory: in a single day in April 1988, American forces destroyed or disabled key Iranian naval assets and oil-platform command posts. But that victory came against an inexperienced, attrited Iranian naval force, and with a huge US posture built for escort, punishment and mine-clearing. 

The sea can decide wars fought on land or in the air - not by defeating the stronger navy outright, but by sinking its strategic objectives

These were relatively limited objectives compared to regime change, and they were backed by a large maritime footprint against an inexperienced, weakened adversary. 

The present problem for US forces is different. Iran has divided its maritime labour between the Nedaja, the regular navy seeking a broader blue-water presence, and the Nedsa, the IRGC navy, which turns the Gulf into a green-water battlespace. 

The Nedaja is a navy of “presence” and “prestige”. The Nedsa is a navy of denial, harassment, ambiguity, redundancy and effectiveness. The former can be found and struck; the latter is designed to be too small, dispersed, numerous and geographically embedded to be cleanly annihilated.

Geography itself, like technology and other macro-level variables, is passive. It can serve blue or red. What matters are tactics, techniques, procedures, system adaptations, munitions innovations and command culture, which can convert geography into coercive power. Iran learned that lesson better at sea than in its own skies. 

An IRGC naval commander described the doctrinal logic of Iran’s asymmetric naval warfare in one line: “We are everywhere and at the same time nowhere.” In operational terms, that means small craft, mines, coastal fires, uncrewed systems, midget submarines, island facilities, and distributed sensors around islands such as Qeshm, Larak, Abu Musa, the Tunbs and Sirri. 

These are not aircraft carriers. They are static maritime bastions and ambiguity engines.

Maritime coercion

Ukraine provides a comparison: the sea can decide a land war. Kyiv lost most of its blue-water naval assets during Russia’s 2014 seizure of Crimea, and by 2022 it had no conventional blue-water fleet with which to confront Russia ship for ship. 

Yet Kyiv used coastal missiles, air-launched cruise missiles, special operations, partisan movements, western intelligence, and uncrewed surface vessels to turn the northwestern Black Sea into a denial zone. 

The results have been strategic rather than merely tactical: Ukraine has sunk or seriously damaged roughly a third of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet’s combat assets, pushed much of the surviving fleet away from Sevastopol, reduced Russia’s freedom of maritime manoeuvre, and reopened a working export corridor from Odesa and other ports. 

In effect, Ukraine did not need command of the sea to sink Russia’s larger strategic objectives: the blockade of Ukraine, coercive pressure against Odesa, the secure use of Crimea as a fleet hub, and the maritime strangulation of the Ukrainian economy.

Iran's way of warfare is being tested to its limits
Read More »

Iran’s Gulf doctrine seeks a mirror-image effect against the US. Tehran does not need to defeat the US Navy ship for ship; it has converted Hormuz, its islands, coastal missiles, mines, drones, fast craft, and small submarines into a theatre where a superior fleet can win tactically, but still lose strategically. 

The lesson is that sea denial is no longer simply a poor navy’s substitute for sea control. In the Black Sea, it helped Ukraine keep a larger sea power from achieving its war aims. In the Gulf, it enabled Iran to “sink” Washington’s strategic objectives without ever winning a classical naval battle.

The comparison might be useful, but these cases are definitely not identical. Ukraine used maritime drones and coastal fires to create theatre-level sea denial, reopen trade routes, and help isolate the occupation forces and their proxies in Crimea. 

Iran used the same family of ideas for chokepoint coercion: not to command the sea, but to threaten access, paralyse insurance markets, delay tankers, strain Gulf air defences, and remind Washington that every air campaign has a maritime bill. Iran’s approach was less a classical naval campaign than an innovative resistance architecture fused with maritime coercion. 

The paradox is therefore simple. Iran lost many tactical exchanges and suffered a series of operational defeats, but it still preserved strategic leverage. The US dominated the skies but could not make the sea irrelevant. 

Ukraine has shown the entire world that a fleet can be beaten without a fleet. Iran has shown that a navy can destroy a superpower’s strategic objectives and shape diplomacy without winning a single naval battle. 

In the age of drones, missiles, mines, non-state forces and distributed targeting, the sea can decide wars fought on land or in the air - not by defeating the stronger navy outright, but by sinking its strategic objectives.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel’s ‘pilot zones’: Withdrawal on paper, continued occupation of south Lebanon
item.description:
Israel’s ‘pilot zones’: Withdrawal on paper, continued occupation of south Lebanon

Submitted by Giovanna Vial on Wed, 08/12/2026 - 15:47
MEE visited two of the villages touted as models for Israel's withdrawal. Residents say Israeli troops were never there to begin with
A Lebanese soldier stands guard at the entrance to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, one of three southern Lebanese villages designated as a “pilot zone” under an Israel-Lebanon framework agreement (Giovanna Vial/MEE)
Off

At the entrance to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, a village in southern Lebanon, a Lebanese Army checkpoint marks the edge of what is now officially known as a "pilot zone".

It is one of three villages - along with Froun and Srifa - designated as such under the framework agreement between Israel, the United States and Lebanon, signed in June 2026.

On paper, the pilot zones, whose implementation began on 20 July, are meant to work as a formula: a gradual Israeli withdrawal, paired with a handover of sovereignty to the Lebanese Army, and the end of Hezbollah's armed presence in these locations.

But Daniel Meier, professor of political science and director of the Master in Middle Eastern Studies at Sciences Po Grenoble, says Israel has sought to use the mechanism for a different purpose.

"Israel sees these pilot zones as another tool to undermine any possibilities for Hezbollah to continue in the south of Lebanon, and not for withdrawing its army," he said.

"The main goal for them is to use the pilot zones to continue their occupation and slow down to the maximum their withdrawal from south of Lebanon.’"

Standing at the Lebanese Army checkpoint in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh (West Zawtar), the contradiction at the heart of the agreement is visible in real time: just a few hundred metres away, in Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh (East Zawtar) Israeli forces remain in place, carrying out near-daily demolitions and bombardments. 

Data gathered by Public Works Studio, a Beirut-based research and mapping collective tracking Israeli attacks on Lebanon, documented Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh among the villages targeted by house demolitions, ground incursions, controlled explosions, arson and "tajrif" - the levelling of land with heavy machinery - between late June and late July 2026. 

During Middle East Eye's time on the ground, five explosions coming from Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh were heard, with smoke rising over the horizon.

Coordinating access with the Lebanese Army, MEE was escorted into the centre of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Lebanese armoured vehicles were present along the dirt road leading into the village.

Entire structures were reduced to rubble, evidence of repeated Israeli air strikes on the village, while bullet holes scarring the remaining walls pointed to ground assaults by Israeli tanks.

Yet, contrary to what the scope of the pilot zones might suggest, there were no traces of a sustained Israeli ground presence, nor any signs that soldiers had occupied or lived in the village.

The hallmarks of Israeli occupation documented elsewhere in Lebanon - Hebrew graffiti sprayed across walls, human waste left behind, and residents’ belongings ransacked and strewn about, as seen in villages such as Yaroun and Ayta al-Shaab in 2024 - were nowhere to be found in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh.

Nor could the idea of the village's "return" to Lebanese sovereign control be verified on the ground, despite the presence of the Lebanese military. The main access to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, let alone anything resembling a return to normal life for its residents, remains blocked by the continued Israeli presence in the surrounding area.

"There is no restoration of Lebanese authority while Israeli occupation remains,’" said Meier.

"This is just another trap, another trick in misusing language, misusing words. The ‘pilot zones’ were designed to give some sort of credit to the idea of Lebanese sovereignty restoration while Israel tries to escape its responsibilities and continue its oppressive occupation strategy without any clear endgame."

Uninhabitable 

Abbas Heri, 40, had just returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, his hometown, which he fled in February 2026. 

"As long as they [the Israelis] don't leave Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, there will be no life here in the village," he said, explaining that the main road connecting the village to Nabatieh, the largest city in southern Lebanon, remains inaccessible because of the Israeli presence in Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh.

'The main goal for the Israelis is to use the pilot zones to continue their occupation and slow down to the maximum their withdrawal from south of Lebanon'

– Daniel Meier, professor of political science

"My house is here, but it is unhabitable. Everything is destroyed. And there's no security either. Last night, for example, I slept at some friends' place here in the village, but there were explosions all night long," he said. "In other words, they [the Israelis] are doing something that stops life from continuing, so people can't go back to living here."

The framework agreement between Israel, the United States and Lebanon fails to specify when - or whether - Israel will vacate the broader "buffer zone" it has carved out along the border, an area Israeli officials say they intend to hold for as long as Hezbollah remains armed. 

Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, as well as Froun and Srifa, sit near the outer edge of the "Yellow Line" - the new, self–declared boundary Israel has drawn to mark its zone of military control inside Lebanese territory, and the same line that gives the buffer zone its shape.

Heri spoke with MEE in the central part of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, near a tent where people had gathered around a small makeshift stall selling coffee, water and cigarettes.

"It is because of these injustices that the resistance emerges and endures," Abbas said when questioned about Hezbollah's presence in the village.

"Resistance movements emerge because of injustice. Would you accept someone occupying your home without defending yourself? I mean, under what law would that be acceptable?"

For Lebanese like Abbas Heri, the concept of the pilot zone - much like the framework agreement that produced it - feels abstract, even irrelevant, next to the reality on the ground.

"The West talks about human rights… What human rights? I have a three-year-old daughter who can already tell the difference between the sound of a plane and the sound of an explosion," he said.

"If this was happening in Europe, the state would show up, the police would show up, everyone would show up. They'd film it, they'd do something to look after people's psychological state. Who is going to compensate us for what the Israelis are doing to us, and how?"

No sign of occupation

In Froun, the second "pilot zone" visited by MEE, residents echoed much of what Heri had said. The village used to be just a 10km drive from Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, but the road that once connected the two has been destroyed in Israeli strikes, forcing a detour that now takes more than an hour to complete.

"I cannot understand how our government is negotiating with the Israelis," said Assem Jaffar, an elderly man sitting amid the rubble of what used to be the facade of his house. "I just hope they don't keep negotiating with the Israelis until they leave, until they get out of our territory."

Jaffar lost his daughter, son-in-law and granddaughter to Israeli bombardments. 

"It's not possible to live in Froun today. The ceasefire they claim exists doesn't exist in practice. The resistance isn't attacking Israel, but they keep attacking us."

In Froun, MEE saw the same pattern of destruction found in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. 

Civilian infrastructure has been devastated: the handful of houses still standing stick out against a landscape otherwise flattened by Israeli bombardments. 

Yet there is no sign that the village was ever effectively occupied by the Israeli army - no evidence of the kind of ground presence that would need to be handed over to the Lebanese Army, as its "pilot zone" status implies.

"These villages, so-called pilot zones, have not been occupied by the Israeli army," Meier said, adding that the Lebanese government has been under intense US pressure to embrace President Donald Trump’s vision of a "new Middle East".

"The price, however, is high: accepting to negotiate with Israel and agreeing with pilot zones which actually just reinforce the erosion of Lebanon's sovereignty."

'We, the children of the south'

Abou Ali, a Froun resident who had recently returned to begin rebuilding his home, said the Israeli army never entered his village or Srifa.

"The Lebanese army wasn't here before either. They only came recently to set up a few checkpoints."

It's not possible to live in Froun today. The ceasefire they claim exists doesn't exist in practice. The resistance isn't attacking Israel, but they keep attacking us'

– Assem Jaffar, Froun resident

His account was consistent with what MEE observed on the ground.

There was no Lebanese military presence in Froun itself, only in the surrounding area. At the village’s entrance, MEE found that the checkpoint was manned by Hezbollah rather than the Lebanese Army.

"The agreement they made was a huge mistake," Abou Ali said, referring to the June 2026 framework agreement.

"This government has brought us to where we are today, and we cannot accept this agreement, because it doesn't benefit us in any way.

"We, the children of southern Lebanon, do not accept any kind of negotiation with the Israeli government."

MEE’s visits to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh and Froun, along with interviews with residents and observations on the ground, point to a clear gap between the framework agreement’s premise and the reality in these villages.

Israeli forces destroyed large parts of both, but there was little evidence of the sustained ground presence that the "pilot zones" designation implies.

The agreement creates the appearance of a gradual Israeli withdrawal and a handover of control to the Lebanese Army. In Froun's case, however, there was no sustained Lebanese Army presence to speak of at all.

Meanwhile, the "withdrawals" from these pilot zones have coincided with continued Israeli military activity elsewhere in southern Lebanon, including in the village of Hadatha. 

Territory framed as relinquished in one location exists alongside expanding operations in another, leaving the overall footprint of Israel's presence in southern Lebanon - which makes up about one-fifth of Lebanese territory - largely unchanged.

Israel's war on Lebanon

item.description:

The Iran war may be fought primarily remotely via the air, but its strategic outcome is increasingly being decided at sea.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Opinion: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East
item.description:
Opinion: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East

Nearly three years after the 7 October Hamas attack shattered the illusion of a manageable status quo - one serving US-Israeli interests, while harming Palestinian rights - and midway through President Donald Trump’s second term, the Middle East no longer maps neatly onto the two axes that have defined it for decades.

The region’s fault line long ran between Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” - comprising Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi armed groups, and a battered but defiant Syria under the Assad regime - and the Israeli-inspired “Pax Americana”: an informal architecture of deterrence, normalisation, and military primacy that Washington and Tel Aviv sought to impose through the Abraham Accords, blatant double standards, international law violations and overwhelming force.

Today, a third pole could be emerging: an increasingly institutionalised “Sunni axis” anchored in Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad - with Doha, Cairo, and to a lesser extent Abu Dhabi at its edges. 

Read more: How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East Opinion by Marco Carnelos

item.description:
Iran and Oman defining a temporary route for now, Araghchi says

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi has reiterated that talks with Oman and reopening of Hormuz were “two separate issues”.

In his comments carried by Shahrara News, he said: “Our negotiations with Oman are ongoing. That is a completely separate matter. It is a technical issue concerning the designation of maritime routes in the Strait of Hormuz for the passage of ships.”

“The routes that existed previously are no longer functional, so a new route needs to be defined. For now, we are designing a temporary route, which can then, at a later stage, be turned into a final route.”

Clause 5 of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding—signed between the United States and Iran—assigns Iran a role in the security and future management of the Strait of Hormuz, including mine clearance. Tehran and Muscat have used this clause to form a joint working group and negotiate bilateral management of the waterway.

“We may reach an outcome soon, but I want to emphasise that these negotiations and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are two separate issues. This is a technical negotiation concerning the designation of a maritime route,” Araghchi said.

“Once this route has been determined, whether the Strait will be reopened or not will depend on the fulfilment of other conditions to which the United States must adhere,” he added.
